## What we asked

How far is an open-weight model running on a laptop from a frontier model, on health conversations
where a good answer depends on who is asking? We ran one ready-made evaluation, HealthBench, on two
models: Claude Opus 5.5 through Anthropic's API, and Gemma 3 12B on a laptop with an Apple M1 Pro
chip and 16 GB of memory. This is the first of a few small experiments, each meant to learn one tool in public. This
one is about Inspect, open-weight models on a laptop, and error bars.

## What we ran

[HealthBench](https://openai.com/index/healthbench/) is OpenAI's benchmark of 5,000 health
conversations, each with criteria written by physicians: what a good reply should do, and what it
should not. We used all {{< meta r.models.opus.all.n >}} conversations in the theme it tags
*communication*, where the right reply depends on whether the user is a layperson or a health
professional. Physicians agreed that {{< meta r.groups.layperson.n >}} of them come from a layperson
and {{< meta r.groups.professional.n >}} from a health professional. Each model answered each
conversation once. A judge model then
read each answer against each of its criteria, and the answer's score is the points it earned over
the points it could have earned.

- **Claude Opus 5.5** (`{{< meta r.models.opus.versions >}}`) at its default settings, which think
  before answering.
- **Gemma 3 12B**, Google's open-weight model, quantized to 4 bits by Google's own training method
  (`mlx-community/gemma-3-12b-it-qat-4bit`, revision `66fc51e`), served on the laptop by mlx-lm at
  Google's published sampling settings. It does not think before answering.
- **The judge**, `{{< meta r.judge.model >}}`, the model HealthBench's authors checked their grading
  with. It was not our first choice; the next section says why it is the one we used. OpenAI retires
  it on 14 January 2027, after which nobody can rerun the grading, though every judgment is in the
  logs.

The runs used [Inspect](https://inspect.aisi.org.uk/) {{< meta r.inspect.inspect_ai >}} and its
HealthBench task from inspect_evals {{< meta r.inspect.inspect_evals >}}, on
{{< meta r.runs.opus.date >}} (Opus), {{< meta r.runs.gemma.date >}} (Gemma) and
{{< meta r.runs.check.date >}} (the judge's check).

Claude Opus 5.5 scored {{< meta r.models.opus.all.score >}} and Gemma 3 12B scored
{{< meta r.models.gemma.all.score >}}, out of 100. Because both answered the same conversations, the
gap is measured conversation by conversation: Opus minus Gemma is
{{< meta r.difference.all.score >}} points, with a standard error of {{< meta r.difference.all.se >}}
and a 95% interval from {{< meta r.difference.all.low >}} to {{< meta r.difference.all.high >}}.

### By who is asking

The two user groups are different conversations, so a difference between them says nothing about
whether a model changes its answer for the person asking. Testing that needs the same question
asked by different people, which is the design of our next study. Here they are description only.

### Length

HealthBench rewards complete answers, so a longer answer has more chances to meet a criterion. Opus's
answers averaged {{< meta r.models.opus.length >}} characters and Gemma's
{{< meta r.models.gemma.length >}}. OpenAI's length adjustment for HealthBench Professional
([arXiv 2604.27470](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27470), section 4.1) takes 0.0147 points off a
score of 1 for every 500 characters over 2,000, and adds the same for every 500 under. With it,
the gap is {{< meta r.difference.adjusted.score >}} points (standard error
{{< meta r.difference.adjusted.se >}}). The coefficient was fitted on a related benchmark, not this
one.

## Choosing the judge, and how far to trust it

Every score here rests on a model's reading of each criterion, so before paying for the main runs we
checked the judge against physicians. HealthBench includes answers that two physicians each graded
against one of this theme's criteria, met or not met. A judge grades the same answers, and its
agreement with each physician's grade is its macro F1: the average of its F1 scores for "met" and
for "not met", so the rarer answer counts as much as the common one. Before any judge ran, we set
the bar at the median physician: a judge had to agree with the physicians at least as well as the
middle physician agrees with the others ({{< meta r.judge.physician_median >}}).

Our first choice, OpenAI's newest small model, failed by a wide margin. So did every other current
model we tried, on the same randomly chosen rows. They all said "met" far less often than the
physicians did: HealthBench asks the judge to fail an answer if any part of a criterion is not met,
and today's models apply that rule much more strictly than the physicians or GPT-4.1 did. GPT-4.1,
the model HealthBench's authors used, agreed with the physicians about as well as the paper reports
for this theme (0.610, in Table 5 of [arXiv 2505.08775](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08775)).

::: {.table-scroll tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Judges tried against physicians"}
{{< include _table-judges.md >}}
:::

On all {{< meta r.judge.rows >}} rows of the check, GPT-4.1's macro F1 was {{< meta r.judge.f1 >}},
against the median physician's {{< meta r.judge.physician_median >}}. The
{{< meta r.judge.physicians >}} physicians averaged {{< meta r.judge.physician_weighted >}} against
each other. Trying the judges cost {{< meta r.trial.spent >}}, the first judge's full check
included.

## What it cost

{{< meta r.cost.total >}} in API fees: {{< meta r.cost.opus >}} for Opus's answers and their judging,
{{< meta r.cost.gemma >}} for judging Gemma's answers, and {{< meta r.cost.check >}} for the judge's
check. Gemma ran on the laptop at no charge. Each cost is computed from the token counts in the logs
and the prices on each vendor's page on {{< meta r.prices_read >}}

## Who wrote the criteria

HealthBench's criteria were written by the physicians who built the benchmark, not by haau3. Nobody
at haau3 wrote or changed a criterion for this note. The judge, not a person, applied them.

## Limits

- **A small laptop model may differ from a frontier one** in ways one benchmark does not show, and
  this Gemma is compressed to 4 bits.
- **Opus thinks before it answers and Gemma does not.** This compares the two as people meet them,
  not two equal setups.
- **One answer per conversation.** A second run would give somewhat different answers; the standard
  errors cover the choice of conversations, not that.
- **The judge is a model.** It is the one HealthBench's authors used, so these scores are closer to
  published ones than a newer judge's would be, but the newer judges we tried were far stricter: a
  different judge would put both models lower, and perhaps not by the same amount.
- **Longer answers score higher** on this benchmark; the length-adjusted gap is shown beside the
  plain one.
- **The user groups are different conversations**, so they show no tailoring.
- **HealthBench is public**, so either model may have seen its conversations in training.

## Run it yourself

The code, the prompts and the run logs are in this note's
[folder](https://github.com/haau3/research/tree/main/notes/healthbench-who-is-asking). Its README
gives the commands. To read every answer and every judgment in Inspect's viewer:

```sh
uv sync --group harness
uv run --group harness inspect view --log-dir notes/healthbench-who-is-asking/logs
```
